resources.string: All simulated sensitive data stored on the device and targeted in vulnerability scenarios.
These vectors target sensitive data on the device. You can view all simulated device data in the \'Data Vault\' screen.
Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted in Private Storage
Data written to SharedPrefs, DataStore, SQLite, or files without encryption — readable via root, ADB backup, or forensic tools.
Sensitive Data Stored Unencrypted Outside of Private Storage
Data written to external/shared storage (SD card, Downloads) that any app or attacker can read without root.
Cryptographic Keys Stored Outside of Platform Keystore
Hardcoded or file-based keys that bypass Android Keystore — extractable without device compromise. (Coming soon)
Sensitive Data Hardcoded in the App Package
API keys, passwords, or tokens baked into source code, resources, or native libraries — extractable via static analysis. (Coming soon)
Insertion of Sensitive Data into Logs
PII, credentials, or financial data written to Logcat — readable by any app with READ_LOGS permission or via ADB.
Sensitive Data Not Excluded From Backup
App data included in ADB or cloud backups, allowing sensitive data extraction without root. (Coming soon)
Review the sensitive data below, then trigger the vulnerability vectors to see how the data leaks.
Review the sensitive data below. The secure vectors will safely process the data without leaking it to logs or plaintext files.
Safely logged via Timber with masking!
Check Logcat for OkHttp BODY interceptor leak!
Network executed safely. Body logs are disabled!
Saved securely via Jetpack Security AES-256-GCM!
User Object sent to Analytics SDK!
Sanitized Object sent to Analytics SDK!
These vectors demonstrate writing data to unprotected private storage locations.
These vectors apply the correct mitigation (encryption, etc.) to private storage.
Vector Triggered — Data Written to Disk
Each vector below writes sensitive data to a different unprotected storage location. Trigger a vector, then verify the plaintext content using ADB or a file manager on a rooted device.
Each vector applies the correct mitigation: encryption, access control, or storage relocation. The underlying sensitive data is never written in a recoverable plaintext form.
Written to shared_prefs/maswe0002_session.xml — plaintext token visible!
Migrated to encrypted DataStore. No plaintext on disk.
Written to files/datastore/ — binary ≠ encrypted. Check Logcat!
DataStore encrypted with AES-256-GCM via Tink. Content unreadable.
Written to databases/maswe0002_vuln.db — check Logcat for WAL path!
Room DB encrypted via SQLCipher. Hex dump shows no plaintext.
content:// URI generated — logged to Logcat. A second app could read this!
FileProvider restricted to images/ only. Traversal URI rejected.
Written to /sdcard/Android/data/…/files/ — visible without root on API < 29!
Redirected to encrypted internal storage. External path not used.
JWT leaked to localStorage via JS. Check /app_webview/
DOM storage disabled or data encrypted.
Plaintext PDF left in cacheDir indefinitely.
PDF encrypted via Tink and wiped securely.
Exported provider allows ../ payload. Attackers can read internal sandbox!
Provider canonicalizes paths and rejects ../ payloads.
Analytics SDK cached PII unencrypted in analytics_shadow.db!
PII masked/hashed before sending to SDK. No plaintext on disk.
Vector Triggered — Data Written to Disk
Data encrypted but key is hardcoded in source — reverse engineer with apktool to extract!
Encryption key generated and stored in Android Keystore. Impossible to extract from APK.
Encryption key stored in /sdcard/…/secret.key alongside encrypted file — trivially extracted!
Key stored exclusively in Android Keystore. Only the app can use it.
Data encrypted with AES/ECB — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks (penguin attack).
Data encrypted with AES-256-GCM. Authenticated, non-deterministic, and secure.
Static key embedded in APK allows data cloned from one device to be decrypted on another.
Key bound to device hardware via Android Keystore. Data cannot be migrated and decrypted on another device.
AES key serialized and written to shared_prefs/crypto_key.xml — plaintext on disk!
Key generated inside Android Keystore. Never leaves the secure hardware enclave.
AES key hardcoded as byte array in source. Extractable with apktool or JADX in seconds.
Key generated at runtime via KeyGenerator and stored in Android Keystore. Never in code.
Key material passed in plaintext to importKey() — briefly exposed in memory and logs.
Key imported using Android Keystore wrapped import API — key material never exposed in plaintext.
API key hardcoded as a String constant — extractable via JADX or strings command on APK.
Secret fetched at runtime from a secure backend. Never present in compiled code.
API key in strings.xml is trivially accessible — apktool decodes resources without needing to decompile Kotlin.
Secrets moved to remote config or Android Keystore. APK contains no sensitive values.
Analytics/push SDK initialized with hardcoded write key bundled in the APK.
SDK initialized server-side or with a short-lived token fetched at launch. No secret in APK.
4. Staging Endpoint / Debug Flag Left in Release
Debug API base URL and logging flag accidentally shipped in the release build — network interceptors could target staging.
Build variants enforce different configs. Release build contains no debug endpoints or verbose logging.
App data included in Google cloud backup by default. Credentials extractable from any signed-in device.
backup_rules.xml excludes all sensitive files and databases from cloud backup.
Sensitive DB exported via `adb backup` — extractable on any laptop without root.
android:allowBackup="false" in Manifest. ADB backup command returns empty archive.
Session tokens and credentials migrate uncontrolled during Google\u2019s device-to-device transfer.
data_extraction_rules.xml disables cloud and device transfer for sensitive files.
Plaintext database included in backup — anyone with the backup file can open it directly in SQLite Browser.
Database encrypted with SQLCipher before backup. Backup file is unreadable without the Keystore-bound key.
Broken algorithms (DES, RC4), reused IVs, ECB mode, weak padding, insufficient key length, or XOR/Base64 passed off as encryption.
MD5 or SHA-1 used where collision resistance is required; plain hash instead of a KDF for passwords; truncated digests.
Improper Use of Message Authentication Code (MAC)
CRC-32 where a MAC is needed; MACs built on weak hashes; fragile constructions; missing replay protection; truncated tags.
Deprecated signature algorithms (SHA1withRSA); insufficient key length; predictable ECDSA nonces; key reuse across purposes.
Verification skipped or result ignored; untrusted/unpinned signer keys; algorithm confusion (accepting \'none\').
java.util.Random in security contexts; time-based seeds; hardcoded or predictable seeds for key generation.
Low-entropy sources; short key lengths; deprecated algorithms; plaintext key export; missing hardware-backing or broad key purpose.
Plain hash instead of PBKDF2/Argon2; too few iterations; missing or predictable salt; low-entropy input (short PINs).
No key versioning; unbounded cryptoperiods; superseded keys not retired — old keys remain usable for new operations.
Keys usable without user auth; key available on locked device; key migrates via backup; unbounded auth validity window.
Sensitive features enabled without checking device lock state; keys not tied to passcode; stale device-lock assumption at runtime.
Data encrypted with DES — key is only 56-bit, broken since 1999. Brute-forced in under 24 hours with modern hardware.
Data encrypted with AES-256-GCM. NIST-approved, authenticated, and computationally infeasible to break.
IV hardcoded to all-zeros. Two ciphertexts encrypted with the same key+IV reveal XOR of plaintexts — full plaintext recovery possible.
Fresh random 16-byte IV generated via SecureRandom for every encryption. IV prepended to ciphertext.
AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with observable error response. 128 requests per byte — full plaintext recoverable via padding oracle attack.
AES-GCM authenticates ciphertext before decryption. Padding oracle attacks are impossible.
AES/ECB used — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. Data patterns fully visible in ciphertext.
AES-GCM used — each block is unique, authenticated, and indistinguishable from random.
64-bit AES key used — far below the 128-bit minimum. Brute-forceable with modern hardware.
256-bit AES key. Provides 128-bit security strength — infeasible to brute-force.
Same RSA key used for both encryption and signing. Cross-protocol attacks can break one use case using the other.
Separate keys generated for encryption and signing. Key separation enforced per NIST SP 800-57.
Data "encrypted" with XOR and encoded as Base64. Trivially reversible — provides zero security.
Real AES-256-GCM encryption with Keystore-backed key. Not reversible without the key.
MD5 used to verify file integrity. Collision attacks known since 2004 — attacker can produce two files with the same hash.
SHA-256 used. No practical collision attack exists. NIST-approved for all integrity use cases.
Password stored as SHA-256(password). Fast hash — 10 billion guesses/sec on a GPU. Offline cracking trivial.
Password hashed with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (310,000 iterations + random salt). GPU cracking reduced by 6 orders of magnitude.
SHA-256 output truncated to first 4 bytes (32 bits). Birthday attack finds collision with only ~65,000 hashes.
Full 256-bit (32-byte) SHA-256 output retained. 2^128 work required to find a collision.
CRC-32 used to "verify" message integrity. An attacker can compute any CRC-32 value — trivially forgeable.
HMAC-SHA256 used. Forgery requires knowledge of the secret key — computationally infeasible without it.
HMAC built on MD5. MD5 is broken — potential length-extension and collision vulnerabilities affect derived MACs.
HMAC-SHA256 used with proper key. SHA-256 has no known collision vulnerabilities.
8-byte MAC key reused across all messages. Low entropy — brute-forceable. Key reuse violates key-separation principles.
256-bit key generated fresh per session via SecureRandom. Not reused across algorithms or purposes.
MAC computed over plaintext, then plaintext encrypted (MAC-then-Encrypt). Vulnerable to padding oracle + chosen-ciphertext attacks.
AES-GCM used — encryption and authentication are atomic. Equivalent to Encrypt-then-MAC, immune to padding oracles.
GCM tag truncated to 4 bytes. Attacker has 1-in-4-billion chance of forging a message — feasible with automation.
Full 128-bit GCM tag used. Forgery probability is 2^-128 per attempt — computationally infeasible.
Valid authenticated message captured and replayed. Server accepts it — no way to distinguish replay from fresh request.
Message includes incrementing sequence number covered by MAC. Replayed messages rejected as sequence already seen.
Document signed with SHA1withRSA. SHA-1 is broken for signatures — collision attacks enable signature forgery.
SHA256withECDSA used. NIST-approved, provides 128-bit security, faster than RSA.
512-bit RSA key. Factorable with public cloud computing in hours. Any attacker can forge signatures.
2048-bit RSA or P-256 ECDSA used. Meets NIST minimum for signatures through 2030+.
ECDSA nonce k hardcoded to 1 for two different messages. Private key fully recoverable with simple algebra from two signatures.
Nonce derived deterministically per RFC 6979. Same nonce never reused. Private key cannot be extracted.
4. Same Key for Signing and Decryption
RSA key pair used for both decryption and signing. Cross-protocol attacks can recover private key material.
Separate RSA key pairs for encryption and signing. Key separation per NIST SP 800-57 enforced.
verify() called but return value not checked. App proceeds regardless of signature validity — any tampered payload accepted.
verify() result explicitly checked. Exception thrown and operation aborted if signature is invalid.
Public key for verification fetched from the same payload being verified. Attacker replaces both key and data — signature always valid.
Public key hard-pinned in app resources. Verification only succeeds with the expected key — key substitution attacks impossible.
JWT library accepts algorithm from token header including \"alg: none\". Attacker strips signature entirely — token always valid.
Algorithm hardcoded in verification logic. Only RS256 accepted regardless of what the token header declares.
java.util.Random used to generate session tokens. Predictable LCG algorithm — next values derivable from observed outputs.
SecureRandom (CSPRNG) used. Output is cryptographically unpredictable — no known way to predict future values.
Random seed derived from current timestamp. Millisecond-precision — attacker who knows approximate time can reproduce entire sequence.
SecureRandom seeded from OS entropy pool (/dev/urandom). No predictable seed — output is indistinguishable from random.
Random seeded with literal 0x1337BEEF. Entire sequence reproducible by any attacker who decompiles the APK.
SecureRandom() instantiated without explicit seed. JVM/OS provides unpredictable entropy automatically.
AES key derived from device IMEI (15 digits = ~50 bits entropy). Brute-force space far smaller than 128-bit key.
AES-256 key generated by KeyGenerator backed by OS CSPRNG. Full 256-bit entropy guaranteed.
512-bit RSA key generated. Factorable with public resources. All data encrypted with it is compromised.
2048-bit RSA key. Meets current NIST recommendations. Infeasible to factor with foreseeable computing resources.
DES key generated — only 56 effective bits. NIST has disallowed DES since 2005. Brute-forceable in hours.
AES-256 key generated via Android Keystore. 256-bit key, hardware-backed, never leaves the TEE.
AES key exported as raw bytes to a file. Anyone with file access has the key — all encrypted data compromised.
Key exported using Android Keystore key wrapping. Key material encrypted before it leaves the secure environment.
Key generated with KeyPurpose.ENCRYPT_DECRYPT and SIGN — one key for all operations. Violates least-privilege principle.
Key generated with setKeyPurposes(ENCRYPT_DECRYPT) only. Cannot be misused for signing or key agreement.
Encryption key = SHA-256(password). Fast hash — attacker can try billions of passwords per second offline.
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 310,000 iterations and random 16-byte salt. Each guess costs significant CPU time.
PBKDF2 configured with 1 iteration. Effectively a plain hash — provides no additional protection over SHA-256(password).
310,000 iterations per OWASP recommendation. Each password guess costs ~100ms — offline attacks become impractical.
KDF salt hardcoded to \"MobSecSalt2024\". Same salt for all users enables precomputed rainbow tables to attack all accounts at once.
Random 16-byte salt generated per user per password. Rainbow tables are useless — each account must be attacked independently.
Encryption key derived solely from 4-digit PIN (10,000 possible values). Offline brute-force completes in milliseconds.
PIN combined with a hardware-bound Keystore secret before KDF. Offline brute-force impossible without device access.
Single hardcoded key version 1. If compromised, all past and future data is at risk. No way to rotate without breaking decryption.
Tink Keyset used with key versioning. New primary key added — old data re-encrypted on next access. Compromise is contained.
Encryption key generated at app install, never rotated. Years of data protected by a single key — long cryptoperiod maximizes exposure.
Key metadata includes expiry date. App checks expiry on launch and rotates expired keys automatically.
3. Old Keys Still Usable for Encryption
After rotation, old key v1 remains active for encryption. New data still encrypted with the compromised key.
Superseded keys demoted to decryption-only. All new encryptions use the current primary key. Old keys eventually destroyed.
Keystore key created without setUserAuthenticationRequired(). App unlocked — any process with app UID can use the key.
Key created with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) + setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(-1). Each use requires fresh biometric.
Key has no device-lock restriction. Background service can decrypt sensitive data while device is locked — attack surface during theft.
Key created with setUnlockedDeviceRequired(true). Key becomes unavailable the moment screen locks — no background access possible.
Keystore key without device-binding. Google Backup includes key material — restored on new device, data decryptable without original hardware.
StrongBox-backed key. Bound to device hardware — cannot be extracted or migrated. Data unrecoverable on different device.
setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(86400). One biometric scan authorizes all key uses for 24 hours — including by malware.
setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(-1). Each key operation requires a fresh biometric prompt — zero coasting window.
Key in StrongBox but no user auth or unlock requirement. Hardware protects key from extraction but not from misuse by any process.
StrongBox key + setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) + setUnlockedDeviceRequired(true). Hardware + software defense-in-depth.
Payment feature accessible without verifying device has screen lock. On a PIN-less device, any physical access unlocks the vault.
KeyguardManager.isDeviceSecure() checked on feature entry. If false, user is directed to set a device PIN/pattern before continuing.
Encryption keys available even when device has no passcode set. User removes PIN — app continues to protect data with accessible keys.
Key bound with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true). If device passcode is removed, key becomes permanently invalidated.
3. Secure: Check on Every Sensitive Operation
isDeviceSecure() checked only at first launch. User later removes PIN — app never re-checks, continues providing full access.
isDeviceSecure() checked every time a sensitive screen is opened. PIN removal detected immediately — feature blocked until lock restored.
Lack of Authentication on App Components
Unintentionally exported components, missing permissions on IPC, unverified callers, overbroad URI grants, open local ports, and unauthenticated deep links.
Lack of Auto-fill Support for Credential Providers
Login fields incompatible with autofill frameworks, no OTC autofill, missing website association, embedded WebView login, and no passkey/FIDO2 support.
Event-bound biometrics without CryptoObject, weak keystore flags, insecure credential fallback, local-only enforcement, no brute-force protection, hardcoded PINs.
DEVICE_CREDENTIAL permitted for sensitive operations, generic auth policies allowing passcode fallback, ops not bound to biometric-only keystore keys.
Crypto Keys Not Invalidated on New Biometric Enrollment
setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(false), missing biometryCurrentSet, or silent key recreation after invalidation \u2014 new enrollments don\'t revoke access.
High-risk operations (payments, data changes) allowed with initial login assurance only. No step-up, no transaction binding, no server-side enforcement.
Sensitive Data Accessible After Session Termination
Sessions not invalidated server-side, no logout UI, no re-auth on background resume, cached tokens/data retained, and no inactivity timeout.
Lack of Non-Repudiation for Critical Actions
Critical actions confirmed through normal UI only \u2014 no hardware-backed cryptographic binding of the displayed transaction to user approval.
Service exported via default (API < 31 default is exported). Any app can bind and call internal methods.
android:exported=\"false\" set explicitly. Component invisible to all other apps \u2014 cannot be bound or started externally.
Component exported with no permission requirement. Any third-party app can invoke it without any declared relationship.
Custom signature-level permission declared and required. Only apps signed with the same certificate can invoke the component.
Binder service exposes sensitive operations without checking who called. Any app can invoke privileged methods.
checkCallingPermission() / enforceCallingPermission() called at every sensitive entry point. Unauthorized callers receive SecurityException.
FLAG_GRANT_PERSISTABLE_URI_PERMISSION used for entire content directory. Receiver retains access to all files forever.
Single-file URI grant without PERSISTABLE flag. Access automatically revoked when receiver no longer holds it.
Local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:8080 with no authentication. Any app with INTERNET permission can access data via localhost.
Local server requires a session token generated at launch and stored only in app memory. Requests without the token are rejected with 401.
JWT payload decoded and trusted without verifying the signature. Attacker forges arbitrary claims \u2014 any user ID, any role.
RS256 signature verified against pinned public key before any claim is used. Invalid or tampered JWTs are rejected outright.
Password-reset deep link triggers reset for any email passed in the URI. No token, no server confirmation \u2014 exploitable by any app.
Deep link contains a one-time HMAC-signed token. Server verifies token before executing the action. Replayed or forged links are rejected.
1. No Autofill Hints on Login Fields
Login EditText has no autofillHints. Password managers cannot identify the field \u2014 users must type credentials manually every time.
AUTOFILL_HINT_USERNAME and AUTOFILL_HINT_PASSWORD set. Password managers auto-populate fields securely without user copy-paste.
2FA code sent by SMS, user must manually read and type it. No OTC autofill hint \u2014 error-prone and slower than necessary.
SmsRetrieverClient + User Consent API used. OTC auto-fills with one tap \u2014 no clipboard exposure, no manual input.
No assetlinks.json or Associated Domains entitlement. Credentials saved for the website are not offered by password managers on the app.
assetlinks.json published on website + android:autoVerify=\"true\" on App Links. Password managers share credentials seamlessly between web and app.
OAuth flow handled in WebView. App can intercept all URLs, inject JavaScript, and read session cookies \u2014 violates OAuth 2.0 BCP.
AppAuth + Chrome Custom Tabs used. Auth runs in a separate process \u2014 app cannot access tokens or intercept the flow.
Password-only login. No passkey option offered. Users resort to weak reused passwords or insecure practices.
Android Credential Manager with passkey support integrated. Users can register and authenticate with device biometrics \u2014 no password needed.
onAuthenticationSucceeded() result trusted directly. Attacker with root or malware can hook the callback to return success without biometric scan.
BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject wraps a Keystore Cipher. The key only unlocks if genuine biometric succeeds \u2014 callback hooking does not help.
Keystore key has no user auth requirement. App process can use key at any time \u2014 including when screen is locked or user is absent.
setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) + validity=-1. Key use requires fresh biometric every single time. No background access possible.
setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(86400). Single device unlock authorizes all key uses for 24 hours \u2014 stolen device = full access.
Validity set to -1. Each key operation requires a BiometricPrompt challenge. No residual auth window to exploit.
Authentication decision made in app code only. Patching the APK or hooking the auth function bypasses protection entirely.
Server validates session token on every API call. Client auth state is irrelevant \u2014 server rejects unauthorized requests regardless of client state.
Custom PIN prompt allows unlimited attempts. 4-digit PIN = 10,000 combinations \u2014 automated brute force completes in seconds.
Failure counter with exponential delay. After 10 failures, encrypted data wiped. Brute force takes years even with automation.
if (pin == \"1234\") { unlock() } \u2014 PIN hardcoded in bytecode. Any decompiler reveals it in seconds.
PIN hashed with PBKDF2 + random salt on setup. Verification compares hash, not plaintext. Decompiling reveals nothing useful.
Authenticator set to DEVICE_CREDENTIAL. Payment authorized with PIN/pattern \u2014 shoulder-surfed or guessed credential bypasses biometric requirement.
Authenticator set to BIOMETRIC_STRONG only. No PIN/pattern fallback \u2014 face or fingerprint required for every sensitive operation.
BiometricManager allows BIOMETRIC_WEAK | DEVICE_CREDENTIAL. Attacker who knows device PIN can fully bypass biometric requirement.
Only BIOMETRIC_STRONG accepted. Enrollment check ensures strong biometric is available before enabling sensitive features.
Biometric prompt shown but sensitive operation proceeds from app logic, not a Keystore key. Callback bypass defeats the protection entirely.
Keystore key created with BIOMETRIC_STRONG and no device-credential fallback. Operation only executes if genuine biometric unlocks the key.
Key survives new biometric enrollment. Attacker enrolls their fingerprint \u2014 their biometric now unlocks the key without the real user knowing.
Key automatically invalidated when new biometric enrolled. App detects KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException and requires re-authentication to restore access.
2. Key Not Scoped to Current Biometric Set
2. Secure: Scoped to Current Biometric Set
Key accessible to any enrolled biometric, past or future. New fingerprint added after key creation = immediate unauthorized access.
Key explicitly tied to biometric set at creation time. Any change to the enrolled biometrics invalidates the key automatically.
App catches KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException and silently generates a new key. Attacker enrolls biometric, app auto-resets, attacker gains access.
On invalidation, user forced through full re-authentication flow (password + 2FA) before new key is generated and old data migrated.
Payment executed using only the session token from initial login. Stolen/leaked session = unauthorized transfers possible.
Payment requires fresh biometric before each transaction. Session token alone is insufficient \u2014 step-up assertion required.
Single biometric approval can be reused for a different transaction. Attacker modifies the amount after approval \u2014 approval still valid.
Transaction hash (amount + recipient + nonce) signed by Keystore key during biometric. Server verifies signature matches the exact transaction.
Biometric shown only in app UI. Server accepts the regular session token without step-up assertion. APK patch skips the biometric entirely.
Server requires a short-lived step-up token in addition to session token. No biometric assertion = API rejects with 403. Unpatchable by client.
4. Same Session for All Risk Levels
Login grants access to everything: balance view, fund transfer, profile change. Stolen session = full account control.
Low-risk ops (balance view) require session only. Medium (profile change) requires PIN. High (transfer) requires biometric + server step-up.
Logout clears local token but server never revokes it. Captured token from network intercept remains valid indefinitely.
Logout calls /auth/revoke endpoint. Server adds token to blocklist. All subsequent requests with the old token return 401.
App has no logout button. Uninstall leaves encrypted data on device. Shared/stolen device retains full session until reinstall.
Logout clears EncryptedSharedPrefs, deletes database, revokes Keystore key. Device reset leaves nothing recoverable.
App backgrounded for 30 minutes and foregrounded without re-auth. Anyone who picks up the unlocked phone has full access.
onResume() checks if last auth timestamp > 5 minutes ago. If so, biometric prompt shown before UI is revealed. Background = safe.
4. Session Token in SharedPreferences After Logout
4. Secure: Complete Local Wipe on Logout
Logout only clears in-memory state. Session token persists in SharedPreferences. Next user of device reads it directly from the file system.
Logout explicitly removes all SharedPreferences keys, clears Room DB, and nulls in-memory state. Nothing persists after logout.
Session stays active forever with no inactivity limit. Unattended device stays logged in indefinitely \u2014 physical access = full access.
UserActivity tracked via MotionEvent. After 5 minutes without input, screen locks and session invalidated. Resuming requires biometric.
1. Critical Action Confirmed Via Normal UI
Fund transfer confirmed via regular AlertDialog. Malware overlaying the screen shows different amount while user taps confirm on actual transfer.
ConfirmationPrompt shown in StrongBox-isolated TEE UI. Malware cannot overlay or modify the displayed message \u2014 what user sees is what gets signed.
Transfer executed with no audit record linking user biometric to the exact transaction. Disputes unprovable \u2014 no evidence of what was approved.
Transaction hash signed by StrongBox ECDSA key during biometric prompt. Server stores signature. Any dispute verifiable with the user\'s public key.
Cleartext network traffic allowed in NSC, HTTP endpoints used, raw unencrypted TCP/FTP/BLE sockets, low level socket API, and third-party library misconfigurations.
Disabled TLS certificate validation, accepting self-signed certificates, missing hostname verification, broken TrustManager, silent error handling, or permissive SDK trust settings.
Misconfigured CertificatePinner, dynamic pins fetched over unencrypted HTTP, custom pinning accepting incorrect certificate chains, or missing backup pins.
1. Cleartext Allowed in Network Security Config
1. Secure: Cleartext Traffic Disabled in NSC
cleartextTrafficPermitted is set to true in network security config allowing unencrypted traffic across the app.
cleartextTrafficPermitted set to false globally in network_security_config.xml.
App endpoints use http:// URLs transmitting sensitive requests and credentials in cleartext.
All network endpoints strictly use https:// scheme with TLS transport encryption.
App uses unencrypted FTP or telnet protocols to exchange files and commands over network.
App uses encrypted transport protocols such as SFTP and TLS-encapsulated socket connections.
Bluetooth RFCOMM or BLE characteristics transmit plaintext payloads without device pairing or app encryption.
BLE payload encrypted at application layer using AES-GCM prior to transmission.
Raw java.net.Socket used directly for network IO without wrapping in SSLSocket.
SSLSocket created via SSLSocketFactory with modern TLS protocols enabled.
Flutter/React Native network engine configured to ignore platform cleartext policies.
Cross-platform network client configured to respect platform security settings and enforce HTTPS.
Analytics or ad SDK uses unencrypted HTTP endpoints by default in background.
All third-party SDKs configured explicitly to transmit telemetry over HTTPS/TLS.
TrustManager configured to ignore certificate validation errors completely.
Default TrustManager validates certificate chain against system CA store.
2. Secure: Validated Trusted CA Certificates Only
TrustManager modified to trust all self-signed or untrusted CA certificates.
Self-signed certificates rejected unless bundled and pinned in trusted KeyStore.
HostnameVerifier overridden with ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER or custom logic returning true.
Strict HostnameVerifier verifies server identity against certificate SAN/CN.
4. Secure: Custom TrustManager Delegation to System
Custom X509TrustManager checkServerTrusted has empty implementation.
Custom TrustManager delegates validation to default X509TrustManager.
5. Secure: Connection Termination on SSL Exception
SSLHandshakeException caught and swallowed allowing network flow to proceed.
SSLException causes immediate request cancellation and aborts operation.
6. Secure: Third-Party SDK Strict Trust Policy
Third-party SDK configured with custom permissive SSLSocketFactory.
Third-party SDK configured to use default platform SSLSocketFactory.
CertificatePinner configured with mismatched domain pattern or incorrect pin hash format.
CertificatePinner configured with valid leaf and intermediate SPKI hashes for exact domains.
2. Secure: Dynamic Pins Over Authenticated Channel
Pins updated at runtime by fetching remote JSON over HTTP without signature verification.
Dynamic pins fetched over HTTPS with digital signature verification prior to updating local pins.
3. Secure: Strict SPKI Certificate Chain Match
Custom certificate pinning logic checks certificate subject string instead of public key hash.
Pinning verifies SubjectPublicKeyInfo SHA-256 hash against expected pin set.
Only single leaf pin defined; key rotation causes complete app bricking.
Primary leaf pin configured along with backup CA/intermediate pins for smooth rotation.
Sensitive Native Functionality Exposed in WebViews
WebViews Allow Access to Local Resources with Untrusted Content
Unnecessary Exposure of Sensitive Data via the User Interface
Unnecessary Exposure of Sensitive Data via Notifications
Insufficient Protection of Sensitive Data from Screenshots or Screen Recordings
Sensitive Data Leaked via Accessibility Services
6. Secure: Strict URI Scheme & Host Check
Running on a Recent Platform Version Not Ensured
Use of Deprecated APIs or Functionality
Using Non-Standard APIs for Security-Critical Functionality
Malicious Code Included in the App
App integrity is not verified against tampered APKs.
App integrity is verified against signature and checksum.
App integrity relies only on local client checks.
App integrity is validated remotely via server endpoints.
Play Integrity token is not verified on backend.
Play Integrity token is cryptographically verified on trusted backend.
4. Secure: Modern APK Signature Scheme v2/v3/v4
App uses legacy APK signature scheme v1 only.
App enforces APK Signature Scheme v2+ with rollback protection.
Internal storage files are loaded without checksum validation.
Internal storage files are integrity checked using HMAC/SHA-256.
Downloaded assets/dynamic files are processed without signature checks.
Downloaded assets are verified with signed hashes before usage.
Backup/restored app state is accepted blindly without validation.
Restored app data is sanitized and revalidated upon initial load.
Failed integrity check results are logged but execution continues.
Failed integrity checks immediately halt execution and invalidate session.
1. Secure: Active Runtime Memory Integrity Checks
No runtime memory checks exist to detect modified code sections.
Runtime checksum checks verify executable code segments in memory.
Loaded dynamic shared objects (/proc/self/maps) are not checked.
/proc/self/maps is scanned for unexpected injected dynamic libraries.
Frida/Xposed hooking framework artifacts are not detected.
Hooking frameworks like Frida and Xposed are detected and blocked.
